prerequisites: No prior C at Chapter 1; each later chapter assumes earlier course lessons, not prior Linux or C expertise.
method: Read authored headings, explanations, instructions, expected outputs and feedback in course order. Check changed actions against editable source and available controls. Retain correct sentences. Inspect and run selected revised experiments; use the full compiler suite for unchanged program fixtures. This is editorial and functional review, not a learner comprehension study.

changes.before: Before iteration i, sum equals the sum of a[0..i), and 0≤i≤n. It holds initially with an empty prefix. Adding a[i] and incrementing i preserves it. changes.after: Before iteration i, sum equals the sum of the prefix a[0..i), meaning indices 0 through i−1, and 0≤i≤n. It holds initially with an empty prefix. Adding a[i] and incrementing i preserves it. The measure n−i decreases, so the loop terminates; at i=n, the invariant gives the required total. Values are small here so the int sum is representable.

changes.before: Inorder visits left subtree, node, and right subtree. For a binary search tree with distinct keys, this produces ascending order. changes.before: The fixture compares a three-node right chain with a balanced three-node tree. Both satisfy BST ordering and have the same inorder sequence, but maximum path lengths differ. For n sorted insertions into a naive BST, the final height is n; an AVL invariant keeps height O(log n).
changes.after: The fixture compares a three-node right chain with a balanced three-node tree. Both satisfy BST ordering and have the same inorder sequence, but maximum path lengths differ. For n sorted insertions into a naive BST, the final height is n; an AVL tree keeps each node’s child heights within one level of each other, giving O(log n) height.

changes.before: A V×V adjacency matrix reserves Θ(V²) entries and tests one edge in O(1). An adjacency list uses Θ(V+E) storage and scans actual neighbors. This matrix fixture uses zero for absent edges, so it cannot represent a zero-weight edge; a more general format needs a separate presence flag or sentinel.
changes.after: Let V count vertices (nodes) and E count edges (connections). A V×V adjacency matrix reserves Θ(V²) entries and tests one edge in O(1). An adjacency list uses Θ(V+E) storage and scans actual neighbors. This matrix fixture uses zero for absent edges, so it cannot represent a zero-weight edge; a more general format needs a separate presence flag or sentinel.

changes.before: BFS explores by edge distance using a queue; DFS follows one path at a time using recursion or a stack.
changes.after: Breadth-first search (BFS) explores by edge distance using a queue. Depth-first search (DFS) follows one path at a time using recursion or a stack.

changes.before: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes a zero-indegree vertex and decrements its outgoing neighbors. If fewer than V vertices are emitted, a cycle prevents completion. The fixed array queue is safe because each vertex enters only when its indegree becomes zero, once. Different available zero-indegree choices can produce different valid orders.
changes.after: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes a vertex with zero indegree (no remaining incoming edges) and decrements its outgoing neighbors. If fewer than V vertices are emitted, a cycle prevents completion. The fixed array queue is safe because each vertex enters only when its indegree becomes zero, once. Different available zero-indegree choices can produce different valid orders.

changes.before: main keeps the Job object alive while the worker accesses it and joins before reading its result. Passing the address of a loop variable reused by all workers can create both a lifetime or synchronization problem and incorrect logical inputs. Thread-local variables and separate per-worker objects simplify ownership but do not automatically protect genuinely shared objects.
changes.after: main keeps the Job object alive while the worker accesses it and joins before reading its result. Passing the address of a loop variable reused by all workers can let workers read changed inputs. Concurrently modifying that variable also needs synchronization, and leaving its scope too early ends its lifetime. Thread-local variables and separate per-worker objects simplify ownership but do not automatically protect genuinely shared objects.

diagram_recommendations.quote: Every level contributes Θ(n) work, and the tree has Θ(log n) levels. Count leaves separately from the total number of nodes; for the example’s power-of-two input, there are n leaves and 2n−1 nodes.
diagram_recommendations.question: Why does splitting eight inputs produce fifteen calls but only eight leaves?
diagram_recommendations.show: Start with one call of size eight at depth zero. It creates two calls of size four at depth one, then four calls of size two at depth two, then eight calls of size one at depth three. Size-one calls are leaves. Adding the call counts gives fifteen; the final depth has eight leaves. The table counts calls, not elapsed time or merge operations.
diagram_recommendations.placement: Immediately after the conceptual explanation, before the worked example.
diagram_recommendations.replaces: Can replace the repeated sentence “This program counts the split tree only” by carrying that scope in the figure note. Keep the recurrence and the merge-combine work assumption in prose.
diagram_recommendations.caveat: This is the power-of-two split fixture. A merge-sort combine step adds work not counted by this program.

diagram_recommendations.quote: For obstacle-free grid paths moving right or down, ways[r][c] depends on the cell above and the cell to the left.
diagram_recommendations.question: Which two previously computed cells contribute to the destination’s six paths?
diagram_recommendations.show: In a three-by-three grid indexed from zero, ways[1][2] is three and is immediately above ways[2][2]. ways[2][1] is three and is immediately to its left. Their arrows converge on ways[2][2], whose value is six. A final down move comes from the upper cell; a final right move comes from the left cell. These two last-move cases are distinct.
diagram_recommendations.placement: Immediately after the conceptual explanation, before the worked example.
diagram_recommendations.replaces: Replaces “The table itself is the dependency diagram.” The revised walkthrough names the bottom-right output and its incoming moves.
diagram_recommendations.caveat: Only right and down moves are allowed; the original grid has no obstacles. Blocking a cell changes these counts.

diagram_recommendations.quote: For each item, visit capacities downward so best[w−weight] still refers to the solution before this item. Updating upward would solve an unbounded-use variant instead.
diagram_recommendations.question: Which earlier write would let an upward update use the same item twice?
diagram_recommendations.show: Consider only the first item, with weight two and value three; every best cell initially holds zero. Descending capacities visit four before two: best[4] reads the old best[2] of zero and becomes three, then best[2] becomes three. Ascending capacities visit two first: best[2] becomes three, then best[4] reads that changed cell and becomes six. Six counts the same item twice, so it belongs to an unbounded-use variant.
diagram_recommendations.placement: Immediately after the conceptual explanation, before the worked example.
diagram_recommendations.replaces: Can replace “Each item contributes at most once because capacities descend” with the first-item trace. Keep the explanation of capacity5=7, the state definition, and the complexity caveat.
diagram_recommendations.caveat: This isolates the first item of the fixture. Capacities count weight units; best values count value units. Upward updates solve a different, reusable-item problem.

diagram_recommendations.quote: The teaching estimate charges one unit per page, assumes a cold cache and one distinct data-page fetch per match, and adds three index levels.
diagram_recommendations.question: When do scattered matches make index navigation plus row fetches cost more than a scan?
diagram_recommendations.show: The model has one hundred table pages and an index with three levels. It charges one page unit for each index level and one distinct data-page fetch per matching row. For one match, the index costs three plus one, or four units, versus one hundred for a scan, so choose the index. For ninety-eight matches, the index costs one hundred and one units, versus one hundred for a scan, so choose the scan.
diagram_recommendations.placement: Immediately after the conceptual explanation, before the worked example.
diagram_recommendations.replaces: Replaces the generic query-pipeline figure on this lesson. The two numeric walkthrough sentences can be replaced by the named narrow= and wide= output interpretation; keep the cost assumptions and result-equivalence rule.
diagram_recommendations.caveat: Cold cache; each match needs a different data page. These are estimated page units, not measured disk reads or timings; both paths must return the same rows.

diagram_recommendations.quote: The fixture has seven score-one rows and one score-nine row. A ten-value uniform model estimates 0.8 matches for score one, while a per-value histogram records seven.
diagram_recommendations.question: Why does a histogram estimate seven matches when a uniform model estimates less than one?
diagram_recommendations.show: There are eight score rows: seven have score one and one has score nine. A uniform model over ten possible score values predicts eight divided by ten, or zero point eight matches for either queried value. A histogram counted from the same rows predicts seven matches for score one and one match for score nine, equal to the actual counts in this fixture. The row total is eight in both cases.
diagram_recommendations.placement: Immediately after the conceptual explanation, before the worked example.
diagram_recommendations.replaces: Replaces the two quoted numeric setup sentences with the comparison table. Keep the data-refresh and correlation caveats.
diagram_recommendations.caveat: The histogram is built from this fixed data. Later updates can make it stale, and single-column counts do not capture correlations between fields.

diagram_recommendations.quote: DBL_MIN is the smallest positive normal double, not the most negative value and not the smallest positive subnormal. On the explicitly required binary64 target with gradual underflow, nextafter(0,1) produces the smallest positive representable value.
diagram_recommendations.question: Which threshold separates a positive normal value from a subnormal value, and when can halving produce zero?
diagram_recommendations.show: Read the boxes in increasing value, starting at zero. Zero is followed by the smallest positive subnormal, two to the power minus one thousand seventy-four. Half of DBL_MIN is two to the power minus one thousand twenty-three and remains subnormal. DBL_MIN is two to the power minus one thousand twenty-two and is the smallest positive normal binary64 double. Halving the smallest positive subnormal rounds to zero under round-to-nearest. The picture shows value categories, not proportional distances.
diagram_recommendations.placement: Immediately after the conceptual explanation, before the worked example.
diagram_recommendations.replaces: Can replace “Half of DBL_MIN remains a finite subnormal on these targets” and “Halving the smallest subnormal through scalbn rounds to zero under the chosen rounding mode” with the ordered boxes and their note. Keep target, rounding, classification, and math-error reporting assumptions visible.
diagram_recommendations.caveat: The experiment requires binary64, gradual subnormals, and round-to-nearest. Boxes are not to scale; the C classification functions determine the printed results.
